---
title: "Setup"
subtitle: "Three ways to run the labs"
---

Every lab runs in three places. **Google Colab** is the default and needs nothing but a
Google account. You can also run the labs **locally** with `uv`, or on an **AWS** GPU
instance. No lab needs API keys or paid services.

## Google Colab (default) {#colab}

1. Open a lab from its module page or the [notebooks page](/notebooks.qmd) with **Open in Colab**.
2. Run the first cell (**Setup**). On Colab it installs exactly what the lab adds (a pinned
   `gymnasium`, `stable-baselines3` or `trl`, and this workshop's `prl` package) and keeps
   every package Colab already has, including PyTorch. It prints the versions and the runtime.
3. Run the cells in order. Each exercise has a `# TODO` cell, a folded Hint and Solution, and a
   checkpoint.

Almost every lab is designed for Colab's default **CPU** runtime. The Module 12 stretch and
one capstone option are designed for a **T4 GPU** (Runtime → Change runtime type → T4 GPU).
A free T4 is not guaranteed on Colab's free tier.

If the setup cell says a package changed version, use Runtime → Restart session and run it
again.

## Your own machine {#local}

You need [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) and Git. On Windows, use WSL 2 and follow the
Linux steps.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/project-delphi/practical-rl.git
cd practical-rl
uv sync --group notebooks          # Python 3.13, CPU PyTorch, the lab packages, prl (editable)
uv run --group notebooks jupyter lab notebooks/
```

The setup cell checks versions instead of installing (`uv` owns your environment) and warns
if anything differs from the pins. On Apple silicon the labs use the CPU by default: small
networks run faster there than on the GPU (MPS).

To run your copy against an NVIDIA GPU on Linux, sync the CUDA build of PyTorch instead:
`uv sync --group notebooks --group gpu --no-group cpu`.

## AWS GPU instance {#aws}

For a dedicated T4 GPU, `infra/aws/` in the repository creates one EC2 `g4dn.xlarge`
instance per participant with CloudFormation. It has no open inbound ports: you reach
JupyterLab through AWS Systems Manager port forwarding. It stops itself after about 90
minutes of idle time, and one command tears everything down. Facilitators can create and
destroy instances for a whole cohort.

See [`infra/aws/README.md`](https://github.com/project-delphi/practical-rl/blob/main/infra/aws/README.md)
for prerequisites (an AWS account, the AWS CLI v2, the Session Manager plugin, and GPU
quota), costs with their source and date, and step-by-step commands. SageMaker AI Studio is
documented there as an alternative.

::: {.callout-warning}
The AWS path has not yet been run end to end; that is a human item on the release checklist.
The [readiness page](/readiness.qmd) says what has run where.
:::

## Check your setup {#check}

Run [Module 0](/modules/00-setup.qmd). Its checkpoints confirm the runtime, and its last cell
prints a **run record** you can send to your instructor.
